description: Speed, velocity, acceleration, motion graphs, and stopping distances — including v² = u² + 2as.
content_html:
Speed and Distance

Speed tells you how fast an object is moving. It is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction. The equation for speed is:

$$v = \frac{s}{t}$$

where \(v\) is speed in m/s, \(s\) is distance in metres (m), and \(t\) is time in seconds (s). This rearranges to \(s = vt\) and \(t = s/v\).

Key Fact

Typical speeds to know: walking ≈ 1.5 m/s, running ≈ 3 m/s, cycling ≈ 6 m/s, car in town ≈ 13 m/s, car on motorway ≈ 30 m/s, train ≈ 55 m/s, sound in air ≈ 330 m/s.

Velocity and Displacement

Velocity is the vector equivalent of speed: it has both magnitude and direction. Two cars travelling at 30 m/s in opposite directions have the same speed but different velocities.

Displacement is similarly the vector equivalent of distance — it is the net distance from the starting point in a specific direction. An athlete who completes one full lap of a 400 m track has travelled 400 m (distance) but has a displacement of 0 m (they ended where they started).

Acceleration

Acceleration is how quickly an object's velocity changes. The equation is:

$$a = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

where \(a\) is acceleration in m/s\(^2\), \(v\) is final velocity in m/s, \(u\) is initial velocity in m/s, and \(t\) is time in seconds. A negative value of \(a\) means the object is decelerating.

A bus accelerates from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 seconds. Calculate the acceleration.

\(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{16 - 4}{6} = \frac{12}{6} = 2\) m/s\(^2\)

Now suppose the bus then brakes from 16 m/s to rest in 8 s: \(a = \frac{0 - 16}{8} = -2\) m/s\(^2\) (deceleration of 2 m/s\(^2\)).

Key Fact

For uniform (constant) acceleration, use:

$$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$

where \(s\) is distance travelled in metres. This equation is essential when time is not given or needed.

A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes uniformly to rest over a distance of 50 m. Calculate the deceleration.

Known: \(u = 20\) m/s, \(v = 0\) m/s, \(s = 50\) m.

\(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\)

\(0 = 400 + 2a \times 50\)

\(100a = -400\)

\(a = -4\) m/s\(^2\) (deceleration of 4 m/s\(^2\))

Time was not given and was not needed — this is exactly when \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) is the right tool.

Distance-Time Graphs

A distance-time graph shows how far an object has travelled over time. Key features: a horizontal line means stationary; a straight diagonal line means constant speed; a steepening curve means increasing speed (acceleration).

The speed at any point equals the gradient of the line: \(\text{speed} = \frac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}}\). For a straight line, pick two points far apart and divide the rise by the run. For a curve, draw a tangent at the point of interest and find its gradient.

Velocity-Time Graphs

A velocity-time graph is even more powerful. The gradient gives the acceleration. The area under the line gives the total distance travelled.

A horizontal line means constant velocity (acceleration = 0). A line sloping upward means increasing velocity (positive acceleration). A line sloping downward means decreasing velocity (deceleration). Complex shapes can be split into triangles and rectangles to find the total area (= total distance).

A common method for measuring acceleration is to use a trolley on a ramp with a light gate connected to a data logger. The independent variable is the force applied (e.g. by varying the hanging mass); the dependent variable is the acceleration. Controlled variables include the total mass of the system. The light gate measures the time taken for a card of known width to pass — from this, both speed and acceleration can be calculated. Results plotted as acceleration against force produce a straight line through the origin if \(F = ma\) holds.

Graphs and Calculations: Exam Technique

When interpreting motion graphs, look at the gradient first. A flat line on a distance-time graph means the object is stationary; a flat line on a velocity-time graph means constant velocity with zero acceleration. Steeper gradients indicate faster speed or greater acceleration. To find displacement from a velocity-time graph, calculate the area under the line. A common exam error is confusing the gradient, which gives acceleration, with the area, which gives displacement, on a velocity-time graph.
exam_tip_html: The most common error in motion calculations is choosing the wrong equation. Use \(a = (v - u)/t\) when time is given; use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) when time is absent. For graph questions: on a distance-time graph, gradient = speed; on a velocity-time graph, gradient = acceleration and area under the line = distance. Always include units in your answer — marks are awarded specifically for correct units. When describing motion from a graph, describe each distinct section separately (e.g. “from 0 to 5 s the object accelerates uniformly; from 5 to 10 s it travels at constant velocity”).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Speed (scalar) and velocity (vector) both measure how fast an object moves; velocity includes direction. Displacement (vector) measures net distance and direction from start to finish. Acceleration = rate of change of velocity = \((v - u) / t\).
  • On a distance-time graph, gradient = speed. On a velocity-time graph, gradient = acceleration and area under the line = distance travelled.
  • For uniform acceleration without time: use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). This is the equation to reach for when a question gives initial speed, final speed and distance — but not time.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between speed and velocity. Give an example to illustrate your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: speed is a scalar quantity (magnitude only); velocity is a vector quantity (magnitude and direction).
1 mark: valid example, e.g. a car travelling at 20 m/s north has the same speed as one travelling at 20 m/s south, but different velocities.

practice_questions.text: A sprinter accelerates from rest to 9 m/s in 1.5 s. Calculate the acceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
\(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{9 - 0}{1.5} = 6\) m/s\(^2\)

1 mark for correct substitution.
1 mark for correct answer with unit (m/s\(^2\)).

practice_questions.text:
A velocity-time graph shows a straight line from (0 s, 0 m/s) to (10 s, 30 m/s), then a horizontal line from (10 s, 30 m/s) to (20 s, 30 m/s).
(a) Calculate the acceleration in the first 10 seconds.
(b) Calculate the total distance travelled in 20 seconds.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(a = \frac{30 - 0}{10} = 3\) m/s\(^2\) [1 mark]

(b) Distance in first 10 s = area under triangle = \(\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 30 = 150\) m [1 mark]
Distance in next 10 s = area under rectangle = \(10 \times 30 = 300\) m [1 mark]
Total = 150 + 300 = 450 m [1 mark]

Common error: using \(v \times t\) for the first section instead of finding the area of a triangle.

practice_questions.text: A train enters a station at 25 m/s and decelerates uniformly to rest. The braking distance is 625 m. Calculate the deceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\):
\(0 = 25^2 + 2a \times 625\)
\(0 = 625 + 1250a\)
\(1250a = -625\)
\(a = -0.5\) m/s\(^2\) (deceleration of 0.5 m/s\(^2\)) [4 marks: 1 for equation, 1 for correct substitution, 1 for rearrangement, 1 for answer + unit]

Note: time was not given — \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) is the appropriate equation.

practice_questions.text: Describe how you could use a ramp, trolley and light gate to investigate how acceleration depends on the resultant force. Identify the independent, dependent and one control variable.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: names equipment without linking to variables.
Secure:
- Independent variable: resultant force (varied by changing hanging mass on a pulley).
- Dependent variable: acceleration (measured from light gate timing data).
- Control variable: total mass of trolley + masses kept constant.
- Method: release trolley from rest; light gate records time for known-width card to pass through two gates; calculate speed at each gate; acceleration = change in speed ÷ time between gates (or use data logger). Repeat for different forces; plot acceleration vs force.

[1 mark: independent variable correctly identified with method; 1 mark: dependent variable correctly identified; 1 mark: valid control variable; 1 mark: clear method showing how acceleration is actually measured]

practice_questions.text: Scientists use mathematical models to predict the motion of moving objects. Explain, using the equations of motion as an example, how mathematical models in science can be useful and what their limitations might be.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states models are used to make predictions.
Secure: the equations of motion (e.g. \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\)) are a simple mathematical model — they can predict the speed and position of an object if acceleration is known and constant; this has real applications in transport engineering and spacecraft design.
Limitations: the model assumes uniform (constant) acceleration — in reality, air resistance and engine force change as speed changes, so the model breaks down for objects accelerating over long distances or at high speeds.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that models are always tested against real measurements; when predictions match observations closely, the model is said to be valid, but a single clear discrepancy can expose a limitation and prompt model refinement (IaS3).

[1 mark: model can predict speed/position given initial conditions; 1 mark: real application; 1 mark: identifies assumption of uniform acceleration; 1 mark: explains when this breaks down; 1 mark: links to testing models against data / IaS3]

left: Horizontal line on a distance-time graph

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between distance and displacement?
flashcard_questions.a: Distance is scalar (how far travelled); displacement is vector (net distance and direction from start).
v = s / t (speed in m/s, distance in m, time in s).

flashcard_questions.q: Give the equation for acceleration in terms of initial and final velocity.
flashcard_questions.a: a = (v - u) / t (acceleration in m/s², velocities in m/s, time in s).

flashcard_questions.q: Give the equation for uniform acceleration that does not involve time.
flashcard_questions.a: v² = u² + 2as (velocities in m/s, acceleration in m/s², distance in m).

flashcard_questions.q: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
What does a horizontal line on a velocity-time graph indicate?
What is the typical speed of sound in air?
A car brakes from 30 m/s to rest in 10 s. What is the deceleration?
Why is velocity a vector but speed is a scalar?
flashcard_questions.a: Velocity includes direction as well as magnitude; speed only gives magnitude.

glossary_terms.definition: How fast an object is moving — the distance it travels per unit time. Speed is a scalar quantity, measured in m/s.
Speed in a specified direction — a vector quantity measured in m/s.
The straight-line distance from an object's starting point to its current position, together with the direction — a vector quantity measured in metres.
The rate of change of velocity, measured in m/s². It is a vector quantity — a negative value indicates deceleration.
A graph with distance on the y-axis and time on the x-axis; the gradient (slope) gives the speed.
A graph with velocity on the y-axis and time on the x-axis; the gradient gives acceleration and the area under the line gives the distance travelled.
